description: We are a team consisting of maths, physics and computer science from Surrey Maths School, who are hoping to turn real-world aerospace physics and orbital mechanics into an interactive, browser-based simulation.
summary:
Project M.A.A.S.A (named after it's creators) is an interactive, browser-based spaceflight simulation built through Python, Github and Streamlit.

We have developed a educational game in which the user designs their own space mission. This takes place through multiple phases, with the user initially selecting a launchpad to take off from, as well as a target celestial body. During the next phase, they select different parts of their vehicle and attempt to balance, mass, research score, and the upthrust provided by different engines. During the next few phases, they encounter interactive minigames such as a physics based launch angle game where the user attempts to curve their orbit around multiple objects and reach their destination planet, as well as another game where they balance the planet's g-force with upthrusting their engine to land safely. 

All of these factors are combined in a formula to determine the player's score, resulting in an engaging dynamic between learning about space missions and physics as well as enjoying the webapp.
details:
The Challenge:

Our task was to design an interactive Space Mission Design Game, allowing participants to experience the process of designing and managing a complete space mission, with potential considerations including defining mission objectives, requirements, designing spacecrafts, selecting scientific instruments etc.

This presented the challenges of incorporating real-world physics, data and values into a gamified, engaging and accessible platform as well as designing an educative tool bridging complex space engineering principles with simpler and interactive graphics.

Benefits:

The benefits to this project include it running entirely in a standard web browser via StreamLit, requiring zero downloads, sign-ins or hardware making this game extremely accessible. Our project turns intimidating aerospace engineering and maths into immediate visual feedback. Finally, this project has high replayability, whether through different launch sites, targets, spacecraft components or simply experimenting with the score produced. This allows players to experiment with various engineering trade offs that real engineers will often encounter.

Intended Impacts:

Our intended impact is to inspire young people into physics, maths and engineering through simplifying what is seen as rocket science into an engaging format for students and casual players, where they experiment with designing different missions and strategise during different phases.

Additionally, it allows players to build an intuitive understanding of why real space agencies make compromises in their designs.

Tools:

We came up with a solution involving designing a browser-based interactive simulation built with Python and StreamLit. 

This resulted in us learning how to utilise GitHub, as well as tools such as GitHub Copilot, Terminal commands, and researching different libraries that would allow us to create complex graphics and interactive animations.

We also utilised HTML5 Canvas and Plotl tools to draw our graphics in real time, and all audio was procedurally generated via standard Python math libraries and browser audio APIs.

Creative Aspects:

We made a few creative design choices and engineering workarounds for Project M.A.A.S.A, such as implementing StreamLit to create a real-time game engine, rather than its typical purpose of creating static data dashboards etc. This allowed us to workaround the traditional limitations of a python web app and create smooth, real-time physics and animations in the browser. We also abstracted rocket science into a playable and intuitive "risk vs reward" balance. Finally, the blend between having different phases and dynamic scoring allows for our game to feel unique and educative.

Factors Considered:

We had to consider a balance between the scientific accuracy of the project, vs how playable and engaging it was. This involved balancing real world data (from sources linked below) with simplified arcade style scoring, equations and controls to avoid the game feeling overwhelming.

Our scoring formula should reward smart engineering whilst penalising failed attempts, encouraging players to optimise their designs

Additionally, we had to blend real time feedback updates with general static descriptions to avoid the cluttering the view of the player.
